title: Language core: design patterns in Java
seriesDescription: Singleton, factory, builder, strategy, observer, command and dependency injection in Java. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Singleton (holder idiom, enum, pitfalls), Builder, Strategy with comparators, Observer, Decorator in the I/O library, lambda capture rules and thread-safe creation.
source: Gang of Four; Effective Java (Bloch) items 2, 3, 17; Robert C. Martin: SOLID; JLS 15.27.2 (lambda capture); java.io decorator classes; Refactoring.Guru; Baeldung

questions.prompt: Write a thread-safe, lazily initialised Java singleton class `Config` using the initialization-on-demand holder idiom (or an enum).

checks.label: constructor is private (or it is an enum)
exposes it via getInstance or the enum constant

questions.explanation: The JVM initialises the `Holder` class lazily and exactly once, which makes it thread-safe without synchronization. `enum Config { INSTANCE }` is the Effective Java answer and also survives serialization and reflection. Double-checked locking needs a `volatile` field.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class `Pizza` with a required `int size` and an optional `boolean cheese`, constructed through a nested static `Builder` class (fluent setters and a `build()` method).

checks.label: has a nested static class Builder
Pizza constructor is private and takes the builder

questions.explanation: `Builder` avoids telescoping constructors and lets you validate in `build()`. A record plus a builder, or a generated builder, gives the same result.

questions.prompt: Write a Java class `Subject` with `subscribe(Consumer<String>)` and `publish(String)` so that publishing calls every subscriber with the message.

checks.label: keeps a collection of Consumer subscribers

questions.explanation: `CopyOnWriteArrayList` lets a subscriber unsubscribe during notification; a plain `ArrayList` would throw `ConcurrentModificationException` then. An unsubscribe method avoids leaks.

questions.prompt: Given a `List<String> words`, write one Java statement that sorts it by string length by passing a `Comparator` strategy to the list.
questions.explanation: `words.sort((a, b) -> a.length() - b.length())` works too; the `Comparator` is the interchangeable strategy.

questions.prompt: Select all genuine drawbacks or pitfalls of the Singleton pattern.

options.text: It is hidden global state, which makes unit tests order-dependent and hard to mock.
options.why: A well-known criticism; prefer injecting a single shared instance.

options.text: Double-checked locking without a `volatile` field can publish a half-built object.
options.why: The classic broken variant before the Java 5 memory model fix.

options.text: Separate class loaders can each create their own instance.
options.why: Singleton means one per class loader, not one per JVM.

options.text: Serialization or reflection can create a second instance unless guarded.
options.why: `readResolve` or an enum singleton prevents this.

options.text: A Java enum singleton can be duplicated through `Constructor.newInstance`.
options.why: The JDK refuses to reflectively instantiate enum types.

options.text: A singleton can never be initialised lazily in a thread-safe way.
options.why: The holder idiom does exactly that.

questions.explanation: In Spring, beans are singletons per container by default, but they are managed by the container and injected, which avoids most of the global-state problems.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Java `enum` with one constant is a safe way to implement a Singleton.

whys.a: Both true, but implementing interfaces is not why it is safe; safety comes from JVM-guaranteed one-time instantiation and protection against reflection and serialization.
whys.b: Correct: both statements are true, yet R does not explain A.
whys.d: A is true; Effective Java recommends this approach.

questions.explanation: Limitation: the `enum` cannot extend another class, and it is eagerly loaded when the `enum` class initialises.

questions.prompt: In `new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream(file))`, which design pattern is `BufferedInputStream` an example of?

options.why: Correct: it wraps another `InputStream`, implements the same abstraction and adds buffering.
Nothing here limits the number of instances.
No subscribers are notified of anything.
The code constructs objects directly with new; no creation is deferred to a subclass.

questions.explanation: The `java.io` readers and streams are the textbook decorator chain: each layer adds one capability.

options.text: `Compile error: i must be final or effectively final`
options.why: Correct: the loop variable changes each iteration, so a lambda cannot capture it.

options.text: It compiles and the tasks print `3, 3, 3`
options.why: That would be a late-binding bug; Java rejects the capture instead.

options.text: It compiles and the tasks print `0, 1, 2`
options.why: Capturing a changing local is not permitted, so there is no output to print.
The list is not modified while it is iterated.

questions.explanation: Copy the value into a final local (`final int n = i;`) or use a stream such as `IntStream.range`.

questions.prompt: A singleton `Config` is created with the initialization-on-demand holder idiom, and its constructor increments a static counter created. Three threads each call `Config.getInstance()` five times. What is the value of created at the end?
questions.explanation: The nested `Holder` class is initialised once, in a thread-safe way, by the class initialisation rules, so the constructor runs exactly once.

questions.prompt: Complete the sentence about the holder idiom.
questions.text: The first call to getInstance() triggers initialisation of the nested {1} class; class initialisation is {2} by the language runtime, so no explicit synchronized is needed, and the instance field is declared {3}.
questions.explanation: Lazy and thread-safe without locking: the runtime serialises class initialisation.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: The Builder pattern is useful when a constructor would otherwise take many optional parameters.
questions.reason: Telescoping constructors are hard to read, while a builder names each argument at the call site.

whys.a: Correct: the readability of named setters is exactly why Builder replaces long constructors.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: the readability of named setters is exactly why Builder replaces long constructors.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: the readability of named setters is exactly why Builder replaces long constructors.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: the readability of named setters is exactly why Builder replaces long constructors.

questions.explanation: Effective Java item 2: consider a builder when faced with many constructor parameters.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: The Observer pattern decouples a subject from its concrete observers.
questions.reason: The subject must know the concrete class of every observer it notifies.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is true, but R is false: the subject depends only on a small observer interface.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is true, but R is false: the subject depends only on a small observer interface.
whys.c: Correct: A is true, but R is false: the subject depends only on a small observer interface.
whys.d: This option says A is false and R is true, which does not match: A is true, but R is false: the subject depends only on a small observer interface.

questions.explanation: The subject sees an interface (or a lambda) and never the concrete observer type.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A Singleton class needs a public constructor so that clients can obtain its instance.
questions.reason: A Singleton guarantees that only one instance of the class exists.

whys.a: This option says both statements are true and R explains A, which does not match: A is false because the constructor is made private; R correctly states the guarantee.
whys.b: This option says both statements are true but R does not explain A, which does not match: A is false because the constructor is made private; R correctly states the guarantee.
whys.c: This option says A is true and R is false, which does not match: A is false because the constructor is made private; R correctly states the guarantee.
whys.d: Correct: A is false because the constructor is made private; R correctly states the guarantee.

questions.explanation: Clients obtain the instance through a static accessor, never by calling the constructor.
